section.title: Final Instructions and Greetings
section.sectionRationale: The apostle's last recorded words are intensely personal: a longing for Timothy to come, the names of those who left and those who stayed, a cloak and the parchments, and a warning about Alexander. Yet at the heart of the loneliness stands the great confession of the letter's end. When no one stood with Paul, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him, delivered him from the lion's mouth, and would bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom. The letter closes as it must, with grace.
section.thesis: Deserted by some and cherishing the few who remained, Paul asks Timothy to come and entrusts final instructions; but the ground of his hope is that when no one stood with him the Lord stood by him, delivered him, and would bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom, to whom be the glory forever.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the call to come, with those who deserted and those who stayed; the warning about Alexander and the lonely first defense; the Lord who stood by Paul and will bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom; and the closing greetings and grace.

units.label: Come to me
units.note: those who left, those who stayed

verses.text: Make every effort to come to me quickly,
because Demas, in his love of {{aion|this world}}, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia.
Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is {{euchrestos|useful}} to me in the ministry.
Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus.
When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the {{membranai|parchments}}.
Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds.
You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message.
At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them.

But the Lord {{paristemi|stood by}} me and {{endynamoo|strengthened}} me, so that through me the {{kerygma|message}} would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.
And the Lord will {{rhyomai|rescue}} me from every evil action and bring me safely into His {{epouranios|heavenly}} kingdom. To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus.
Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus.
Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers.
The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.

aion.gloss: An age, an era, the present world order in its passing form. Demas deserted Paul because he loved this present age, the world as it now is rather than the age to come. His tragedy is not a single sin but a settled affection: he set his heart on what is fading instead of on Christ's appearing, and so let go of the apostle and the gospel.

euchrestos.gloss: Useful, serviceable, profitable for good use. Paul once refused to take Mark on a journey, yet now, years later, calls him useful for ministry. The word marks a restored and proven servant, showing that failure need not be final and that the Lord makes the once-rejected fruitful again in His work.

membranai.gloss: Parchments, prepared animal-skin sheets used for the most valued and durable writings, a Latin loanword. Facing death, Paul still wants his books and especially the parchments, most likely portions of Scripture. Even at the end the apostle hungers for the word of God, showing that no maturity outgrows the need to keep reading and being shaped by Scripture.

paristemi.gloss: To stand by, to come to one's side, to be present as a helper. When every human supporter deserted Paul at his defense, the Lord Himself took the place beside him that no one else would take. The word paints a courtroom scene in which the risen Christ stands as the advocate and companion of His servant when all others are gone.

endynamoo.gloss: To put power into, to strengthen from within. The Lord did not merely stand near Paul; He infused him with strength for the task. The same power that raised Christ sustains His servant, so that the message could be proclaimed even from the dock, and human weakness became the stage for divine strength.

kerygma.gloss: The proclamation, the thing preached, the announced message of the gospel. Paul's chief concern at his trial was not his own safety but that the kerygma be fully proclaimed so all the Gentiles might hear. Even in chains the gospel was not bound; God used the apostle's danger to carry the message further, showing that the message matters more than the messenger's comfort.

rhyomai.gloss: To rescue, to deliver, to draw someone to oneself out of danger. Paul is certain the Lord will rescue him from every evil deed, not by sparing his life but by bringing him safely through death into the heavenly kingdom. The rescue he expects is final and complete: not escape from dying but deliverance into glory.

epouranios.gloss: Heavenly, belonging to heaven, above. The kingdom into which Paul expects to be brought is not of this passing age but the heavenly kingdom of Christ. Set against Demas who loved this present world, Paul's hope is fixed on the world above, so that death is the doorway into the kingdom that cannot fade.

basic.context: These are the closing lines of Paul's last letter. He urges Timothy to come to him soon, because he is largely alone: Demas has abandoned him out of love for the world, others have gone on assignments, and only Luke remains. He asks Timothy to bring Mark, and to bring his cloak and his books, especially the parchments. He warns about Alexander, who did him great harm, and recalls that at his first trial no one supported him. But then comes the high point: the Lord stood by him, strengthened him so the gospel could be fully preached, delivered him, and will bring him safely into the heavenly kingdom. Paul ends with greetings and the blessing of grace.
basic.hermeneutics: Even the most personal parts of Scripture teach us. The names and requests are real history, but they reveal how the gospel holds a man at the end of his life. The lesson is not that we must fetch a cloak, but that Christ stands by His people when everyone else fails, that He is faithful to bring them home, and that His grace is the last word.
basic.originalLanguages: Demas loved the aion, this present age. Mark is now euchrestos, useful, for ministry. Paul wants his membranai, the parchments. When all deserted him, the Lord did paristemi, stood by him, and did endynamoo, strengthened him, so the kerygma, the proclamation, would be fully made. The Lord will rhyomai, rescue him, into His epouranios, heavenly, kingdom.
basic.typology: Paul's deliverance from the mouth of the lion recalls God's rescue of His servants like Daniel, and points to the final deliverance of all the faithful. The advocate who stands beside the accused foreshadows Christ our advocate before the Father.
basic.christ: Christ is the Lord who stood by Paul when no one else would, the strength by which the gospel was proclaimed, and the King whose heavenly kingdom is Paul's sure destination. He is the faithful friend of the deserted and the rescuer who brings His servants safely home through death.
basic.god: God receives the glory forever as the one who never abandons His servant. When human faithfulness fails, His does not. He strengthens the weak, uses their trials to spread His word, and guarantees their arrival in His kingdom, so the last note of the letter is doxology and grace.
basic.crossReferences: Second Timothy 1 remembers Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of Paul's chains. Psalm 22 speaks of being saved from the mouth of the lion. Matthew 28 promises Christ's presence to the end, the promise Paul proves true here.
basic.oneStory: God has always kept His people to the end, standing with them when the world deserts them and bringing them safely home. Paul's lonely cell becomes a window on that faithfulness: the Lord stands by His servant, carries the gospel forward through him, and welcomes him into the heavenly kingdom. The story of redemption ends not in the desertion of friends but in the presence of Christ and the triumph of grace.

context.literary:
This closing section is built like a letter home from prison, and its structure is easy to miss because it looks like a list. It runs in three rhythms. First comes a set of requests, verses 9 to 13: come quickly, bring Mark, bring the cloak and the scrolls. Woven through the requests is a roll-call of people, and the verbs do the work: Demas has deserted, Crescens has gone, Titus has gone, Tychicus I have sent. Only Luke is with me. A reader can feel the room emptying.

Second comes a pair of reports, verses 14 to 18, built around two courts. The first is the quarrel with Alexander, a matter for Timothy to beware of. The second is the first defense, where everyone deserted Paul, and here the narration turns on a single conjunction at the start of verse 17: "But the Lord stood by me." The contrast with the desertion of verse 16 is the hinge of the whole section. Where "everyone deserted" there is one who did not, and the verse that follows shows what His presence achieved. The thought then leaps forward to a promise, verse 18, and breaks into a doxology: "To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen."

Third comes the sign-off, verses 19 to 22, a string of greetings in the manner of the ancient letter, with names that appear nowhere else. The final blessing is notable for a change of number. "The Lord be with your spirit" is addressed to one person, Timothy, while "Grace be with you all" uses the plural and so reaches the whole community that will hear the letter read.

Placed at the end of the letter, the section shows the same truth the earlier chapters teach by command: faithfulness in a time of abandonment is possible because Christ is faithful. The personal details are not a break from the theology but its demonstration. The pattern of desertion and presence is also set against the opening of the letter, where Paul remembers Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of his chains, 1:16-18, and so the letter is framed by examples of loyalty and loneliness.
context.historical:
Paul writes from Rome in what appears to be his last imprisonment, and the details of the letter give a glimpse of the apostle's world. He asks Timothy to come before winter, verse 21, because sailing on the Mediterranean in winter was dangerous or closed, and a delay of a season could mean arriving too late. Troas, where he left his cloak with Carpus, was the harbor town on the northwest coast of Asia Minor, and Paul had passed through it more than once, Acts 20:5-6. The cloak, a heavy outer garment, would matter in a cold Roman cell, and the scrolls, especially the parchments, were precious: the word "parchments" in the Greek is a Latin loan word, membranae, a reminder that the empire's languages had crossed into Paul's own vocabulary. Whether those were copies of Scripture or his own papers, we are not told.

The companions are a small map of the early mission. Demas had been with Paul in Rome earlier, Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24, and now he has left for Thessalonica out of love for the present age. Crescens went to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia, on the Adriatic coast, probably on missions. Tychicus was a trusted courier and had carried letters before, Ephesians 6:21 and Colossians 4:7. Mark, who had once left the first journey and caused a sharp parting between Paul and Barnabas, Acts 15:37-39, is now called useful to Paul in the ministry, a sign that the old rift had healed.

Alexander the coppersmith cannot be identified with confidence. Alexander was a common name, and the New Testament has more than one man called that, so it is wise to say only what the letter says: a man who did Paul serious harm and opposed the message strongly. "The first defense" refers to an earlier hearing in Rome, where Roman practice allowed the accused to be supported by advocates and friends. No one appeared, and Paul says that no one stood with him.

The final greetings name Prisca and Aquila, the couple from Rome who had worked beside Paul at Corinth and Ephesus, Acts 18:2-3 and Romans 16:3-5, and Onesiphorus's household. Erastus may be the Corinthian official of Romans 16:23. Trophimus, an Ephesian, had been with Paul on his last visit to Jerusalem, Acts 20:4 and 21:29. Pudens, Linus and Claudia are otherwise unknown in the New Testament, and they show that a small Roman church was still serving the prisoner.
context.canonical:
The deliverance Paul describes is told in the language of the Psalms and the prophets. "The mouth of the lion" recalls David, who was delivered from the lion and the bear, 1 Samuel 17:37, and the cry of the sufferer in Psalm 22:21, "Save me from the mouth of the lion." Daniel in the den is the great example, Daniel 6:20-22, where the king asks whether Daniel's God has been able to deliver him, and Daniel answers that God sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths. Paul stands in the long line of those who have been brought through a mortal threat by the Lord.

The experience of being deserted and yet upheld has its deepest Old Testament parallel in the psalms of the afflicted. The righteous sufferer says that father and mother may forsake him but the Lord will take him up, Psalm 27:10. And the Lord's presence with His servants in danger runs through the book of Acts: a vision in Corinth, "I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you," Acts 18:9-10, and a night visit in the barracks, "Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome," Acts 23:11. In each case Paul's strength is the Lord standing near.

The prayer for Alexander's repayment has its own history. Paul speaks in the manner of the psalmists who commit judgment to God, and with Romans 12:19 in the background: "Vengeance is Mine, I will repay, says the Lord." The prayer for those who deserted him, "May it not be charged against them," recalls Stephen's prayer, Acts 7:60, and the Lord's word from the cross, Luke 23:34. Mercy for those who failed is set beside justice for the one who opposed.

The promise that the Lord will rescue him and bring him into His heavenly kingdom links to the Lord's Prayer, "deliver us from the evil one," Matthew 6:13, and to the hope of the whole New Testament. The doxology belongs with those in Romans 11:36 and Galatians 1:5. Paul ends where the church ends all its hopes, in praise.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants Timothy to come, and he wants him to know what to expect. The tender requests are not filler; each carries a human need. He is lonely, cold and short of books. He asks for Mark because Mark has become useful to him, and the request is a quiet commendation of a man who once failed. He speaks of Demas without bitterness but without softening, so that Timothy sees what the love of the present age costs.

The account of the first defense is meant to prepare Timothy for what may happen to him. The charge in the previous chapter was to preach and to suffer. Here Paul shows what it looked like when he did, including the loneliness, and he shows it through the lens of what the Lord did. He does not say, "I was brave." He says, "The Lord stood by me." The point Timothy is to take is that his own courage will not come from within.

The warning about Alexander is plain and practical: be careful of this man. It is not an invitation to personal revenge, since Paul has just prayed that the desertion of others not be held against them. And the close, with its ordinary greetings, tells Timothy that the letter's high themes belong to the same world as ordinary friendships. The gospel is carried by named people, with real names, who are greeted by name, and the church that is grace-filled is also a place of faces.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything here is description: who went where, what was left in Troas, who sent greetings, who was left sick. The details are inspired history, but they are not rules. We are not told to collect cloaks for prisoners, though the care of those in need is taught elsewhere, nor to expect every ministry to end in abandonment, nor to treat the case of Trophimus as a doctrine about illness.

What is prescribed is brief. Timothy is told to come, to bring Mark, and to beware of Alexander. The first two are particular to his situation. The warning to beware of an opponent of the message is a sensible habit for any church leader, with the limits that the passage itself sets: it comes with a refusal to repay evil with evil, and it speaks of a man who has actively opposed the gospel, not of someone who merely disagreed.

The lasting teaching lies in the testimony of verses 17 and 18. Paul reports what the Lord did and what He will do. Those verses are description in the form of confidence, and they invite the same confidence in the reader. They do not promise that every believer will be spared death, and Paul himself expects to die, 4:6. They promise that the Lord will be present and will bring His people home.

debates.question: What is 'the mouth of the lion' from which Paul was delivered?

views.label: A figure for mortal danger, drawn from the Psalms and Daniel
views.case: Psalm 22:21 and Daniel 6 give the picture of a rescue from a deadly threat. Paul may be using a familiar biblical image for the narrow escape at his first hearing, when the verdict could have been death.

views.label: The emperor or the Roman power
views.case: Some ancient readers took the lion as Nero, or the Roman court, since the words follow the first defense. The image of a lion for a hostile ruler has biblical precedent, as with Daniel's lions and the lion of Proverbs 19:12.

views.label: The devil
views.case: Others point to 1 Peter 5:8, where the devil prowls like a roaring lion, and take the phrase as a spiritual deliverance. The parallel with the preceding line about rescue from every evil deed also suits a wider reading.

debates.bearing: The text says only that Paul was delivered, and that he expects to die soon, so the image cannot mean escape from death for good. Whether the lion is danger, empire or enemy, the point of the verse is the same: the Lord stood near and the message got through.

debates.question: Why was Trophimus left sick in Miletus, and what does it say about healing?

views.label: Healing was never guaranteed, even for apostles
views.case: Paul had performed healings, Acts 19:11-12, yet he left a close companion sick. Elsewhere he speaks of Epaphroditus's grave illness, Philippians 2:25-27, and tells Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments, 1 Timothy 5:23. The pattern suggests that healing was a gift given as God willed, not at the apostle's command.

views.label: Apostolic healing was a sign that faded in its use
views.case: Some argue that the gift of miraculous healing was concentrated in the early apostolic period and that the later letters show it in decline. They point to the way Paul treats illness in these late letters as a matter for care and prayer.

views.label: The text does not tell us
views.case: The note is an incidental fact in a list of movements. It is risky to build a doctrine on one line, and the verse says only that Trophimus was sick and was left.

debates.bearing: Whatever one concludes about healing today, the verse shows that sickness and faithful service can go together, and that the apostle did not see a sick friend as a spiritual failure. The passage honors the sick companion by naming him.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 10 says that Demas, "in his love of this world," has deserted Paul. The word for desertion is egkataleipo, to leave behind or abandon, the verb that Jesus used on the cross when He quoted Psalm 22:1, "My God, why have You forsaken Me?" Paul uses it again of the people at his first defense in verse 16. In both places the verb marks the pain of being left, and in verse 10 the object, "this world," is the present age, a word that in Paul's writing means the age that is passing away, 1 Corinthians 7:31. The love in question is agapao, the same word used for those who "crave His appearing" in verse 8. The two loves, one for this age and one for His appearing, face each other across the same chapter.

Verse 11 calls Mark euchrestos, useful. The word is built from the roots for well and for use, and it describes someone who serves well. The same word is used of the once-useless Onesimus in Philemon 11, where it is the point of a play on his name. Mark has been reclassified from a liability to an asset, and the form of the word suggests ease of use, a person who can be counted on. The verb diakonia, "ministry," is the ordinary word for service.

In verse 13 the cloak is the phelones, a heavy outer garment, and the "parchments" are membranai, a Latin loan word for skins prepared for writing. The two items were probably chosen with care: warmth for the winter and writing for the work. The bare fact that a man of Paul's standing asked for them should not be spiritualized away. It shows an apostle who needed a coat and a book.

Verse 17 gives the center of the section in two verbs. Paristemi, "stood by," is a word used of a person who takes a place beside another, as an advocate or a friend does in court. It is the very thing the others failed to do at the first defense, where no one stood with him, though Paul uses a different verb for their absence. The Lord took the empty place. Endynamoo, "strengthened," means to put power into someone, and is used of Paul's own testimony in Philippians 4:13 and of the believer's strength in Ephesians 6:10. The grammar of the purpose clause says that the message might be "fully proclaimed" and that all the Gentiles might "hear it." The first verb is plerophoreo, to fill to the full, and it shows that Paul saw his courtroom witness as the completion of the proclamation, a trial that served as a pulpit.

In verse 18 rhyomai, "rescue," is the same verb as in the Lord's Prayer, "deliver us from the evil one," Matthew 6:13. It is the language of being snatched away from danger. The kingdom is described as epouranios, heavenly, a word that in the New Testament often marks the realm where Christ reigns, as in Ephesians 1:20. "To Him be the glory forever and ever" is the Greek idiom of the ages of the ages, the strongest way the language has to say without end.

The final blessing changes pronouns. "Be with your spirit" uses the singular, aimed at Timothy, while "Grace be with you" uses the plural, aimed at all who will hear the letter. The shift moves the closing from one man to the whole church.

typology.fulfillment: David was rescued from the lion and the bear, 1 Samuel 17:37, and Daniel was kept in a den of lions by the God who sent His angel, Daniel 6:22. In each, the rescue is a sign that the Lord keeps those who belong to Him. Paul's rescue is another instance, but with a sharper edge: he expects to die soon, 4:6, and he trusts the Lord to bring him through death into His kingdom, 4:18. The escalation is found in Christ, who went into death itself and came out of it, Acts 2:24, and whose resurrection is the pledge of the believer's final deliverance. The type is incomplete without Him, for the old rescues only delayed death.

typology.type: The one who stands beside the accused
typology.fulfillment: In the court of Rome Paul had no advocate, but the Lord stood by him. The picture echoes the Old Testament hope that God would stand at the right hand of the needy to save him from those who judge him, Psalm 109:31, and the promise in Isaiah 41:10, 'Do not fear, for I am with you.' In the New Testament the Advocate is Jesus Christ the righteous, 1 John 2:1, who speaks for His people before the Father, and the Spirit is another Helper, John 14:16. The correspondence is that the abandoned are never alone. The fullness is that Christ's presence is not only at a trial but forever, Matthew 28:20.

Mark deserted the work at Perga and was refused by Paul at Antioch, Acts 13:13 and 15:37-39, and yet he is now called useful. His story echoes Israel's own pattern of failure and restoration, and, more closely, the way the Lord restored Peter after the denial, John 21:15-17. The correspondence is that failure need not be the last word. The escalation is that restoration rests on Christ's own faithfulness and forgiveness, not on the servant's improvement. The type has a limit: Mark's restoration was among friends, and it is a sign, not the cause, of the grace that gives a second beginning.

study.christ:
The center of the passage is a Person who stands beside a deserted man. "The Lord stood by me" is the Lord Jesus, as the title is used for Him throughout the letter, and Paul's whole account of the trial is a witness to what Christ does for His own. Where everyone left, He remained. This is the promise He made to His disciples: "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you," John 14:18, and "I am with you always, even to the end of the age," Matthew 28:20. Paul is a man who has been given the proof of it.

The Lord's presence in the courtroom has a purpose. He strengthened Paul "so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it." The risen Christ had told Paul at his conversion that he would carry His name before Gentiles and kings, Acts 9:15, and here, before the highest court of the empire, the commission is being carried out. Christ gets His witness even from a prisoner. What looked like defeat for the gospel was in fact its advance, as Paul had said of his chains in Philippians 1:12-13.

There is a pattern of Christ's own experience in the deserted apostle. On the night of His arrest the disciples left Him and fled, Mark 14:50, and He said that they would be scattered, each to his own home, and that He would be left alone, yet He was not alone, because the Father was with Him, John 16:32. Paul shares in that pattern, being left and yet not alone. And Paul's prayer that the desertion not be charged against those who left him recalls the Lord's own prayer for those who crucified Him, Luke 23:34.

Christ is the Rescuer. The deliverance from "every evil action" and the safe arrival in His heavenly kingdom depend on Him, who is "able to save completely those who come to God through Him," Hebrews 7:25. The Lord who stood by Paul in the court will be with him in death, and the Christ who rose is the guarantee that death is not the end of the rescue.

A guard is in order. The passage should not be read as a promise that Christ will always spare His people from suffering or death; Paul expects to die. The point is the nearness of Christ, not exemption from loss. And the many names of the closing greetings are not hidden symbols of Christ. They are real people, the fruit of a gospel that creates a family, and the family belongs to Him.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the God who is present when everyone has gone. The word for His action in verse 17, "stood by," is intimate and personal, and the whole section turns on it. Paul is not describing a distant deity who rewards good conduct in the end, but one who takes a place beside His servant in the hour of need. That is a central claim about who God is: He keeps company with the abandoned.

He is also the God who works through weakness. The strength given to Paul is not for his comfort only but for the advance of the message, and the prison and the court become places where the gospel is heard by the highest and by the many. This shows a God who is not hindered by human failure. The people who deserted Paul did not stop the proclamation, and neither did Alexander's opposition. God's purposes run through and past them. The nations will hear, and the word will be fully made known.

He is just and merciful at once. Paul says the Lord will repay Alexander according to his deeds, an affirmation that wrongs will not go unanswered. Yet he prays that the failure of those who deserted him will not be charged against them. The same God who judges also forgives, and Paul leaves each matter in His hands. This is a pattern of trust: the apostle does not take vengeance, and he does not pretend there is no justice.

He is the one who rescues and brings home. The promise of verse 18 is not a hope that things may go well but a conviction that God will complete what He has begun. The rescue is from "every evil action," and it ends in His kingdom. The fact that the kingdom is called heavenly marks it as secure, beyond the reach of earthly courts.

He is worthy of glory. The doxology at the end is the proper answer to everything in the passage. Paul has recounted loneliness, hostility, desertion and approaching death, and he ends with praise. A God who can be praised in such a place has proved Himself.

For worship, the passage invites honesty and trust together. It lets us name the losses, as Paul does, the empty chairs and the cold cell, and then turn to the one who stands beside us. It teaches that the last word of a believer's story is not abandonment but doxology and grace.

crossReferences.note: Written from an earlier imprisonment, this passage lists Mark, Luke and Demas together, with Luke called the beloved physician and Demas simply named. It lets readers see how far the picture has changed: Demas, once among the companions, has now left, while Luke remains and Mark is welcomed.

The sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas over taking John Mark, who had deserted them in Pamphylia. It is the background to the request in verse 11. The man Paul once refused is now the man he asks for, which shows the healing of an old wound.

Another prison letter in which Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke send greetings as fellow workers. It shows the circle of helpers around Paul at an earlier time and makes the later desertion of Demas more poignant.

Onesiphorus, who often refreshed Paul and searched diligently for him in Rome, unashamed of his chains. He is the bright counterpart to those who deserted at the first defense, and the greeting to his household in verse 19 closes the circle opened in the first chapter.

In Corinth the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision, telling him not to be afraid but to keep on speaking, for He was with him. It is an earlier instance of the same nearness, and it shows that the Lord's standing by Paul in Rome was a pattern of a lifetime.

The Lord stood near Paul in the night and told him to take courage, for he must testify in Rome as he had in Jerusalem. The Lord's standing near him, in a closely related verb, is the same kind of presence, and the promise is the one that brought Paul to Rome, where the trial of 2 Timothy 4:16-17 took place.

The suffering one cries, 'Save me from the mouth of the lion.' The psalm is the great prayer of the abandoned and ends in praise, which makes it the natural background for Paul's deliverance and for the doxology of verse 18.

Daniel's deliverance from the lions' den, in which God sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths because Daniel was found innocent. It is the clearest biblical picture behind verse 17 and shows the Lord's power to keep His servant in the face of a hostile court.

Paul greets Prisca and Aquila, who risked their lives for him, and the church that meets in their house. It explains why their name comes first in verse 19 and shows their long service stretching from Corinth to Ephesus and Rome.

The warning not to love the world, which passes away along with its desires, while the one who does God's will remains forever. It is the best commentary on the case of Demas in verse 10, and it shows the stakes of what a person loves.

The risen Lord's promise to be with His disciples always, to the end of the age. Paul's experience in the Roman court is a particular proof of that general promise, and it is the ground on which the closing prayer 'The Lord be with your spirit' is made.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is a story of presence lost and presence promised. In Eden God walked with His people, and sin drove them out. After that the story is full of small returns: God with Abraham in the night, God with Joseph in the prison, God with Israel in the cloud, God with Daniel among the lions. Each is a glimpse of what the whole story aims at, the day when God will dwell with His people again. This passage places one more of those returns in a Roman prison. When everyone else leaves, the Lord stands by.

The passage also shows the church in its ordinary shape. The people it names are not heroes but a mix: Demas, who loved the present age, Mark, who failed and was restored, Luke, who stayed, and Trophimus, who was sick. The gospel gathers such people into a family and sends them to different places. The mission to the Gentiles, which began in Genesis with the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham, Genesis 12:3, is here being carried by a scattered group of ordinary believers, and by one lonely apostle in chains whose trial becomes a pulpit.

The passage looks back to the long story of the faithful who were rescued and the faithful who were not. Daniel was brought out of the den, and others were sawn in two, Hebrews 11:33-37. Paul belongs among them, and his hope is not a rescue from every danger but a rescue into the kingdom. In that way the story's tension between the rescue in this life and the rescue beyond it is held together by the promise that the Lord will bring His own safely home.

The ending of the letter anticipates the ending of the Bible. A man who has been left by many, and who is soon to die, says the Lord will bring him into His heavenly kingdom and breaks into praise. At the end of the story, the loud voice from the throne says that God's dwelling is with humanity, that He will wipe away every tear, and that death will be no more, Revelation 21:3-4. Paul's cold cell and empty chairs will be answered by that great company, and the grace he asks for in his last line will be seen to have been the whole of the gift.

sermon.title: The Lion's Mouth
sermon.why: Part of Begg's series A Study in 2 Timothy, this message expounds 2 Timothy 4:14-18, showing how, when no one stood with Paul, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him, delivered him from the lion's mouth, and would bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom.

options.text: Because he loved this present world.
options.note: Verse 10 names his love of this present age as the cause of his desertion.

options.text: Because Paul had wronged him personally.
options.note: The text gives no such reason; the cause is love of the world.

options.text: Because he was sent away on gospel work like Tychicus.
options.note: Others left on assignment, but Demas deserted out of love for the world.

options.text: Because his heart was set on the world rather than Christ's appearing.
options.note: True and close, restating his love of this passing age.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about Mark in this passage?

options.text: That he is useful for ministry and should be brought along.
options.note: Verse 11 calls Mark useful and asks Timothy to bring him.

options.text: That he can never be trusted again after failing before.
options.note: The opposite: Paul now calls the once-refused Mark useful.

options.text: That he has deserted Paul like Demas.
options.note: That was Demas; Mark is commended as useful.

options.text: That a servant who once failed has been restored and made fruitful.
options.note: True and close, drawing out the meaning of Mark now being useful.

quiz.q: What happened at Paul's first defense?

options.text: No one stood with him; everyone deserted him.
options.note: Verse 16 records that all deserted him at his first defense.

options.text: The whole church rallied publicly to his side.
options.note: The opposite is true; everyone deserted him.

options.text: He was immediately released and all charges dropped.
options.note: The point is his abandonment by people, not the verdict.

options.text: He was left alone by those who should have supported him.
options.note: True and close, restating that everyone deserted him.

quiz.q: What is the heart of Paul's confidence in verses 17 and 18?

options.text: The Lord stood by him and will bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom.
options.note: Verses 17 and 18 rest on the Lord's presence, strength, and final deliverance.

options.text: That he would surely escape execution and live on.
options.note: His hope is deliverance into the heavenly kingdom, not escape from death.

options.text: That his own courage had never once wavered.
options.note: The confidence is in the Lord who stood by him, not in himself.

options.text: That Christ is faithful to strengthen and finally save His servant.
options.note: True and close, summarizing the Lord standing by and rescuing him.

quiz.q: How does Paul respond to being rescued and kept by the Lord?

options.text: With a doxology: to Him be the glory forever and ever.
options.note: Verse 18 answers the Lord's faithfulness with glory to God.

options.text: With boasting in his own endurance.
options.note: He gives glory to the Lord, not to himself.

options.text: With bitterness toward those who deserted him.
options.note: He asks that it not be charged against them and praises God instead.

options.text: By turning his rescue into praise of God.
options.note: True and close, capturing the doxology that flows from the Lord's faithfulness.

questions: Demas loved this present world and let go of Christ. Where is love for the world quietly pulling at your own heart, and what would it look like to set your hope on Christ's appearing instead?
Paul, once unwilling to take Mark, now calls him useful. Is there someone who failed you, or a way you failed others, where the Lord may be writing a story of restoration?
Even facing death, Paul wanted the Scriptures. What does your hunger for God's word reveal about your heart, and how might you return to it in this season?
When no one stood with Paul, the Lord stood by him. Where do you feel alone right now, and how does it change things to know Christ stands beside His people when others fall away?

Paul answered the Lord's faithfulness with glory to God and left Timothy with grace. As you finish this letter, what would it look like to entrust your own ending, whatever it holds, to the Lord who brings His people safely home?

translationNotes.note: Parchments renders a Latin loanword for prepared animal-skin sheets used for durable, valued writings, most likely portions of Scripture.

Stood by me translates a word for taking one's place beside another as a helper or advocate; the mouth of the lion is a figure for deadly peril, variously understood as Nero, execution, or Satan's assault.
Prisca is a variant of Priscilla; see Acts 18:2, the same couple who labored with Paul.
Some manuscripts (BYZ and TR) add Amen at the close; the BSB text ends with Grace be with you all.
